core_idea: Time is what passes as things happen, measured in seconds, minutes, and years; a time is a period in it, a point in it, or one of the moments when the same thing happens.

senses.definition: what is measured in seconds, minutes, hours, days, and years, and passes as things happen

examples.text: Time seems to pass more slowly when you are waiting.
As time went by, they became close friends.
Over time, the paint had faded to a soft pink.
The time passed so quickly that we missed the last bus.

senses.definition: the minutes or hours that you have available for doing something, or that something needs

examples.text: Do you have time to talk?
There isn't enough time to finish the report today.
It took a lot of time to learn the new system.
I spend too much time on my phone.

adaptation.grammar: Uncountable in this sense: *much time*, *a lot of time*, *some time*, not *many times* or *a time*. **Time to do something** takes a to-infinitive; **time for** takes a noun.

senses.definition: a period of minutes, hours, days, or years, seen as a whole

examples.text: They lived abroad for a time.
It's been a long time since we last met.
She stayed for a short time and then left.
The doctor said the medicine takes a long time to work.

compare.note: **a while** is a short, vague period: *wait a while*

subsenses.definition: a period in the past or in a person's life, with its own ways and conditions

examples.text: In my grandfather's time, most people walked to work.
Times were hard when the factory closed.
We live in strange times.
In earlier times, the river was the only road.

subsenses.definition: the experience that someone has during a period, whether pleasant or unpleasant

examples.text: Did you have a good time at the party?
We had a lovely time by the sea.
The new students had a hard time at first.

items: have the time of your life

senses.definition: the hour and minute of the day, as shown by a clock

examples.text: What time is it?
Do you have the time?
The clock on the wall shows the wrong time.
The flight leaves at nine o'clock local time.

compare.note: **an hour** is a length of sixty minutes; **the time** is what the clock shows

adaptation.false_friends: Several languages ask for the clock time with their word for **hour**; in English, ask *what time is it*, never *what hour is it*.

senses.definition: a particular point in the day, the year, or someone's life, when something happens or should happen

examples.text: It's time to go home.
This is not a good time to ask him.
At the time of the accident, the road was wet.
By the time we arrived, the show had started.

adaptation.grammar: **It is time to go** and **it is time for bed** take no article. After **it is time** and **it is about time**, a past tense means now: *It is time we left.*

senses.definition: an event or moment when something happens, especially one of several that can be counted

examples.text: This is the first time I have been to the mountains.
We have met only a couple of times.
I take the pills three times a day.
Next time, call before you come.

adaptation.grammar: Countable: *three times*, *the first time*. After **this is the first time** or **the last time**, English uses the present perfect (*This is the first time I have driven*), not the present. *Three times a day*, not *three times in a day*.

senses.definition: used after a number to say that another number or amount is multiplied by it, or that one thing is that much bigger, more, or better than another
senses.explanation: In sums, **times** means multiplied by and is written with the sign ×. In comparisons it comes before **as**, **more**, or a comparative: *three times as far*, *ten times more*, *a hundred times better*.

examples.text: Three times four is twelve.
Two times two makes four.
The new hall is three times as big as the old one.
Prices here are ten times higher than at home.

senses.definition: the regular pattern of beats in a piece of music

examples.text: The drummer kept time while the others played.
The dancers moved in time with the music.
This song is in waltz time.

senses.definition: the number of minutes and seconds that someone takes to complete a race

examples.text: She ran her best time of the season.
The winner's time was a new record for the school.
Everyone's times were slower in the heat.

phrases.definition: at the planned time, not late
phrases.explanation: Compare **in time**, which means early enough.

examples.text: The train left exactly on time.
She is never on time for anything.
Please be on time tomorrow; the bus won't wait.

phrases.definition: early enough to do something, or before it is too late
phrases.explanation: **In time** also means after a period has passed, in the end: *In time, the pain went away.* *In time with the music* means with the same beat. Compare **on time**, which means at the planned time.

examples.text: We got to the station in time to catch the last train.
You are just in time for dinner.
In time, she learned to enjoy living alone.

phrases.definition: together, or during one period
phrases.explanation: **At the same time** also introduces a fact that must be kept in mind although it points the other way: *The job is hard; at the same time, I like it.*

examples.text: Everyone started talking at the same time.
The two letters arrived at the same time.
It's an easy job, but at the same time it is boring.
examples.note: introducing a point that goes the other way

phrases.definition: sometimes, but not often or regularly

examples.text: We still see Ana from time to time.
From time to time the old machine stops without warning.

phrases.definition: do something slowly and carefully, without trying to be quick
phrases.explanation: Said to a slow person, **take your time** can show annoyance.

examples.text: There's no rush; take your time.
Take your time over the exam and check every answer.
Take your time, why don't you? We've only been waiting an hour.
examples.note: ironic, to someone who is too slow

phrases.definition: very often, or continuously
phrases.explanation: With a period in mind, **all the time** means during the whole of it: *He was here all the time.*

examples.text: My little brother asks questions all the time.
It rains here all the time in spring.
I knew the answer all the time but said nothing.

phrases.definition: again and again
phrases.explanation: **Time and time again** and **time and again** mean the same.

examples.text: She has proved time after time that she can be trusted.
Time after time the same mistake appears in the reports.

phrases.definition: very quickly or very soon
phrases.explanation: Also **in no time at all**, and **in next to no time**.

examples.text: The children ate the cake in no time.
Don't worry, the doctor will be with you in no time.

phrases.definition: for now, until something changes

examples.text: For the time being, we are staying with my parents.
The office will stay open for the time being.

phrases.definition: sometimes

examples.text: At times the job can be very stressful.
He can be difficult at times.

phrases.definition: in the past, but not now
phrases.explanation: **All at one time** means at the same moment: *Everyone left all at one time.*

examples.text: At one time, the whole valley was covered with forest.
I lived in the city at one time.

phrases.definition: in groups of the number stated, one group after another
phrases.explanation: With a length of time, **at a time** means for whole periods of that length: *for hours at a time*.

examples.text: Please come in one at a time.
She took the stairs two at a time.
He can sit and read for hours at a time.
examples.note: for whole periods of that length

phrases.definition: before the time that was planned or expected

examples.text: The builders finished the job ahead of time.
Let me know ahead of time if you can't come.

phrases.definition: old-fashioned in your ideas or methods

examples.text: The shop is a little behind the times; it still doesn't take cards.

phrases.definition: used to say that time seems to pass very quickly

examples.text: Time flies when you're having fun.
Is it really ten years since we met? How time flies!

phrases.definition: find it difficult or unpleasant to do something
phrases.explanation: Followed by an -ing form (*had a hard time finding it*) or by **with** and a noun. **Have a difficult time** and **have a tough time** are used in the same way.

examples.text: I had a hard time finding your house.
The new students are having a hard time with the language.
She had a hard time after her husband died.

phrases.definition: say unkind things to someone or make things difficult for them, often as a joke

examples.text: My friends gave me a hard time about my new haircut.
The boss gave him a hard time for being late.

phrases.definition: do something to fill a period while you wait for something

examples.text: We killed time at the airport by playing cards.
I had an hour to kill, so I walked around the market.

phrases.definition: used to say that something should have happened before now
phrases.explanation: **It's high time** means the same. Both are usually followed by a past tense that refers to now: *It's about time you got a job.*

examples.text: It's about time you cleaned your room!
The bus is here at last. About time, too!

phrases.definition: at some time long ago
phrases.explanation: The traditional first words of a story for children.

examples.text: Once upon a time, there was a king who had three daughters.
Once upon a time, this street was full of small shops.

phrases.definition: a very enjoyable experience

examples.text: The children had the time of their lives at the fair.

phrases.definition: very much, or on a large scale
phrases.explanation: **The big time** is the highest level of success, especially in sport or entertainment: *a singer who has made the big time*.

examples.text: I owe you big time for this.
He messed up big time.

phrases.definition: always, at every moment

examples.text: Children must be with an adult at all times.

phrases.definition: that has ever lived or existed
phrases.explanation: Used after a superlative: *the greatest of all time*.

examples.text: Many people say she is the best singer of all time.

phrases.definition: spend a period in prison

examples.text: He did time for robbery when he was young.

phrases.definition: get more time to do something by delaying something else

examples.text: The lawyer asked more questions just to buy time.

phrases.definition: try to delay something so that you have longer to get ready or to decide

examples.text: The council is playing for time, hoping the problem will go away.

phrases.definition: the time allowed for something has ended

examples.text: Time's up! Put your pens down.

phrases.definition: used to say that wasting time costs money, so people should work quickly

examples.text: Hurry up; time is money!

phrases.definition: outside your working hours, not while you are being paid to work
phrases.explanation: The usual British form is **in your own time**, which can also mean at whatever speed you choose.

examples.text: Personal calls should be made on your own time.

phrases.definition: have more free time than you need or want

examples.text: Since he retired, he has had a lot of time on his hands.

phrases.definition: travel quickly, without delays

examples.text: The roads were empty, and we made good time.

phrases.definition: used to say that the result of something will be known only later

examples.text: Was it the right decision? Only time will tell.

phrases.definition: used when meeting someone you have not seen for a long time

examples.text: Kim! Long time no see!

phrases.definition: before you were born, or before you came to a place

examples.text: That singer was popular before your time.
The old manager left before my time.

phrases.text: not give someone the time of day
phrases.definition: refuse to speak to someone or to show any friendliness toward them

examples.text: Since the argument, she won't give him the time of day.

word_family.note: measure how long something takes, or choose the moment for it
**schedule** is more common in American English

usage_note: **Time** and **the time** are different: *Do you have time?* asks whether someone is free; *Do you have the time?* asks what the clock says. *What time is it?* asks for the clock time; *How many times?* asks about occasions. Note the prepositions in the fixed phrases: *on time* (not late), *in time* (early enough), *at the time* (then).

learner_errors.incorrect: The bus came in time, at exactly eight o'clock.
learner_errors.correct: The bus came on time, at exactly eight o'clock.
learner_errors.note: **On time** means at the planned time; **in time** means early enough, before it is too late.

learner_errors.incorrect: It's the first time I visit this city.
learner_errors.correct: It's the first time I have visited this city.
learner_errors.note: After **the first time** and **the last time**, English uses the present perfect, not the present.
**What time** asks about the clock; **how many times** asks about occasions.

adaptation.semantic: English uses one word where many languages use three: time as it passes, the clock time (*the hour*), and an occasion (*three times*). Check which sense is meant before translating; the plural **times** almost always means occasions, a period in history, or multiplied by.
adaptation.grammar: Uncountable when it means time passing or available: *much time*, *a lot of time*. Countable for a period, a point, or an occasion: *a long time*, *a good time*, *three times*. Note the preposition in fixed phrases: *on time* (not late), *in time* (early enough), *at the time* (then).
adaptation.culture: In English-speaking countries clock times are usually given with the twelve-hour clock, *seven in the evening* rather than *nineteen hundred*, and being **on time** for work and for appointments is expected; lateness needs a warning or an apology.
adaptation.false_friends: In many languages the word for **time** also means weather; English **time** never does. Several languages ask the clock time with their word for **hour**; English asks *what time is it*, not *what hour*.
adaptation.pronunciation: One syllable with the vowel of **my** and **eye**; the final **e** is silent. **Times** ends with a **z** sound.
